conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. You were admitted directly today to help with nutrition and ulcer treatment. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly awful. I’m nauseated all the time, and I can barely eat. The pain in the middle of my upper stomach is constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’ve been dealing with that. I see you’ve lost about 20 pounds over the last month and you’ve had more vomiting over the last few weeks. Is that still happening daily?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Some days I throw up even if I just try a few bites. I’m trying to drink water so I don’t get dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The plan is to place a tunneled central line today so we can start total parenteral nutrition—TPN—through the vein, and also give your ulcer medicine through the IV to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the line the same as a PICC? And is it permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar purpose, but this one is a tunneled catheter that goes into a neck vein and then under the skin to your chest. It’s meant for longer-term use than a regular IV. It’s not permanent—we’ll remove it when you’re able to meet nutrition by mouth again and no longer need IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about infections. I’ve heard central lines can be dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a very reasonable concern. There is an infection risk, but we reduce it with sterile placement, careful dressing changes, and teaching you how to keep it clean and dry. Home nursing will also help with dressing changes and lab draws.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep for the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get moderate sedation—medication to make you relaxed and sleepy—and numbing medicine at the site. You’ll be breathing on your own, and we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the ulcer—why isn’t it getting better? I’m taking the Protonix and Carafate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your recent endoscopy showed the ulcer is still there but not bleeding. With marginal ulcers after Roux-en-Y, healing can be slow. You’ve been doing the right things—no NSAIDs, no smoking, no alcohol. One thing we can do is keep the acid suppression very consistent by giving Protonix through the IV, and support your nutrition so your body can heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t tolerate my vitamins either. They make me gag.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have Nutrition see you. TPN includes vitamins and minerals, and we can also talk about forms of supplements that are easier to tolerate when you’re ready—like crushed or liquid options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start IV fluids now and a temporary peripheral nutrition while we wait for the tunneled line placement this afternoon. Let us know if your nausea or pain spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something for nausea? It’s constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we’ll give anti-nausea medication through your IV and keep you comfortable. We’ll also continue your ulcer coating medicine, sucralfate, by mouth as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interventional Radiology is ready for you soon for the tunneled line. Any last questions before you go down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt afterward? And where exactly will it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll likely be sore at the neck and chest for a few days. The catheter will come out on the upper chest with a dressing over it. We’ll give you pain control and show you how to protect it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the procedure. The tunneled double-lumen catheter was placed without complications, and it’s ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy. My chest feels tight where the dressing is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected right after placement. We’ll check the site frequently. If you notice increasing pain, swelling, drainage, or fever, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do we start the nutrition through it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tonight we’ll transition from the peripheral nutrition to TPN through the new line. We’ll start at a lower rate and increase daily while monitoring your electrolytes and blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night with the new line and the first TPN run?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept some. I’m still nauseated, but I didn’t throw up overnight. The line site is sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign about the vomiting. We’ll keep adjusting nausea meds. Today we’ll increase the TPN a bit and keep you on IV Protonix every 12 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat at all? Or does that make the ulcer worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can try small amounts as tolerated. The goal is not to force it—TPN is covering your nutrition. We’ll advance your diet slowly and focus on foods that are less irritating. Nutrition will go over a stage-based diet with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition is going to meet with you today. They’ll talk about ways to get calories in without worsening pain—small, frequent, gentle foods—and how TPN will be adjusted to your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll never be able to eat normally again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that. The goal is to use TPN as a bridge—support you while the ulcer heals and nausea improves. We’ll reassess regularly, and you’ll have close follow-up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing today? Any diarrhea or new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No diarrhea. Still nauseated, but I managed a little of the diet yesterday. The pain is still there though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’re increasing the TPN again today toward the goal calories and protein. Your labs look stable, and we’re watching electrolytes closely as we advance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood work—am I malnourished even though my albumin was normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Albumin can stay normal even when intake is poor. We’re looking at the whole picture—your weight loss, how little you’ve been able to eat, and markers like prealbumin. We’re using TPN to reverse the protein-calorie malnutrition and help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helps but it wears off fast. I’m scared of taking too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want your pain controlled safely. Because you’ve been needing frequent doses, we’re going to ask the chronic pain team to see you and recommend a regimen that’s effective and safer. We’ll also coordinate with your primary care provider for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Today is hospital day 3, and you’ve reached the goal TPN rate. Next step is to start cycling it—running it over 16 hours instead of continuously—to see how you tolerate the higher hourly rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does cycling do? Is it just for convenience?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Convenience is part of it—especially at home, many people run it overnight. It also gives your body time off the infusion each day. We do it gradually to make sure your blood sugar and fluid balance stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain team came by. They said something about changing how often I can take my medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They felt your pain wasn’t well controlled on the prior schedule, so they recommended increasing the frequency of your as-needed pain medication. We’ll implement that here, and we’ve notified your primary care provider so they can place the order and refer you to the pain clinic for ongoing management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be labeled as drug-seeking. I just want to function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, and your symptoms and history support that this is real pain from the ulcer. Our goal is comfort and safety, with a clear plan and follow-up so you’re not managing this alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did the first 16-hour cycle go today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was okay. I felt a little flushed when it started, but it passed. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep monitoring your blood sugar and electrolytes. If all stays stable, we can plan for a 12-hour cycle for home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re focusing on discharge planning. You’ve tolerated cycling, and we’re aiming for a 12-hour overnight TPN schedule at home with visiting nurse support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared I’ll mess up the line at home. What if it gets pulled or leaks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get hands-on teaching before you leave—how to keep the dressing clean and dry, how to flush the line, and what to do if the tubing is damaged or the line is pulled. If it’s ever partially or completely pulled out, you should not use it and you should call right away or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How often will someone check on me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home services will provide the TPN supplies, draw labs a few times per week, and change the dressing weekly or sooner if needed. They’ll also be a point of contact for line concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a new dull pain on the right side under my ribs. Is that my gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your weight loss and symptoms, it’s reasonable to check. We ordered a right upper quadrant ultrasound to look for gallstones or gallbladder inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound is back—no gallstones and no signs of acute cholecystitis. There wasn’t a sonographic explanation for the right upper abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then? I’m worried something is being missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s understandable to worry. Sometimes pain can be from the ulcer area, muscle strain, or irritation without a clear ultrasound finding. The reassuring part is there’s no evidence of gallbladder infection or stones. If the pain worsens, moves, or you develop fever, vomiting you can’t control, or black/bloody stools, you should seek care immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still going to be on Protonix through the IV at home? Why not pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—IV Protonix every 12 hours for about two months. The goal is to maximize consistent acid suppression while your ulcer heals, especially since you’ve had trouble tolerating oral intake and you’ve improved on IV therapy before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Carafate—do I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue sucralfate four times a day, and crush it as instructed so it’s easier to take after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my vitamins? I haven’t been good about them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending vitamin D in a crushable form, and the TPN will provide vitamins and minerals while you’re on it. As your nausea improves, we’ll work with Nutrition and your outpatient team to get you back on a bariatric-appropriate vitamin routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will I manage pain at home? I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have liquid oxycodone as needed, with clear safety instructions—no driving, and don’t take it if your breathing rate is very low. You can also use liquid acetaminophen as needed, staying under 4 grams per day. The chronic pain team recommended changes, and your primary care provider will place the referral to the pain clinic so there’s a structured follow-up plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call right away once I’m home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call or come in for fever over 101.5, shaking chills, redness/swelling/drainage at the line site, chest pain or shortness of breath, vomiting where you can’t keep down fluids or meds, signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing, or any blood or black material in vomit or stool. Also call if the line is damaged or pulled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still anxious, but I feel better having a plan. I just want the ulcer to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’ve tolerated the TPN well, your nutrition markers have started to improve slightly, and you’re stable for discharge. We’ll send you home with services for TPN and line care, and you’ll continue IV Protonix and sucralfate. We’ll also arrange surgical follow-up and the pain clinic referral through your primary care provider.
